newsitem.title: USA: U.S. negotiators drop Medicaid cap from budget.
newsitem.headline: U.S. negotiators drop Medicaid cap from budget.

text.p: White House and congressional negotiators working on a balanced budget deal agreed Friday to drop a controversial plan to cap federal spending for the Medicaid health program, sources said.
Democratic aides also said negotiators were now expecting a smaller adjustment in the Consumer Price Index than they had been discussing during Thursday negotiations.

"They dropped the Medicaid per capita cap," a top House Democratic source said. He also said negotiators planned to add more money to any final budget deal to fund President Clinton's domestic spending priorities.

The White House and congressional Republicans have been able to make adjustments to the emerging budget plan due to Congressional Budget Office forecasts of better than expected economic activity, giving them more money to work with.

Sources said the two sides were very close to a final deal. The flurry of last-minute changes to Medicaid and other programs was likely to increase the odds that congressional Democrats would support any final budget deal.

The budget framework under discussion Thursday called for about $25 billion in Medicaid cuts over five years. For the first time, it would have capped federal spending on the program, which provides health care to 37 million poor, elderly and disabled Americans.
Medicaid is jointly funded by the states and Washington.

The National Governors' Association vowed to fight the cap, calling it a huge cost shift to states. They said if annual growth in the program were higher than expected, they would have to increase spending or drop people from the rolls.
On the CPI, the negotiators are now expecting to include a 0.15 percentage point adjustment in the inflation index in their budget estimates, Democratic aides said.

In essence, the negotiators agreed to accept whatever the Labor Department recommends for changing the inflation measure, dropping plans for a higher adjustment that would have required Congress to pass legislation.
They added more money for nondefense discretionary spending, defense spending and a childrens' health initiative.
